summary: Clarifies and generalizes the GSS-API channel bindings facility, which ties authentication to a particular secure channel. It also sets requirements for future GSS-API mechanisms and programming language bindings.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC clarifies how GSS-API channel bindings are represented across programming languages. It defines a shared structure and sets a requirement for new GSS-API mechanisms that support channel bindings.

questions: how do channel bindings prevent man in the middle attacks
how do channel bindings improve security
why do different programming languages need the same channel binding structure
what fields are in gss-api channel bindings
subtitle: A general structure and requirements for GSS-API channel bindings.

tldr.problem: The GSS-API descriptions of channel bindings were incomplete and partly tied to the C language binding.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a generic structure with initiator and acceptor address types and values plus application data, and requires new supporting mechanisms to conform to RFC 5056.
tldr.outcome: It clarifies the channel-binding facility and updates RFC 2743.

today: RFC 5554 is a Standards Track document that updates RFC 2743. It clarifies the generic structure and use of GSS-API channel bindings.

sections.title: Why Channel Bindings Need a Generic Form
sections.content: The GSS-API provides a channel-binding facility, but the base specification treated the bindings as an octet string and left important structure details to its C-language binding. RFC 5554 generalizes those details so they are not specific to C.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier GSS-API descriptions did not define channel bindings in a language-independent way. This RFC describes a generic form that different language bindings can use.

sections.title: The Channel-Bindings Structure
sections.content:
The generic structure contains an initiator address type and address, an acceptor address type and address, and application data. The address-field values are described in the C-bindings specification, while this RFC presents the structure as part of an abstract API rather than a protocol format on the wire.

Mechanisms still encode the structure's contents in a mechanism-specific way. A new language-specific binding SHOULD specify a formulation of this structure. If a binding represents channel bindings as an octet string, it MUST treat that string as the application-data field alone, not as an encoding of the whole structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The structure records address information for both parties and data supplied by the application. It is an API structure, not a message format sent over the network.

sections.title: Requirements for New Mechanisms
sections.content: New GSS-API mechanisms that support channel binding MUST conform to RFC 5056. The RFC also explains that language bindings should use the generic structure rather than define a C-specific form.
sections.plainLanguage: A new GSS-API mechanism that supports channel binding must follow RFC 5056. Language bindings should describe the same general structure in their own terms.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC refers readers to RFC 5056 for general channel-binding security considerations. It also says that language bindings using an octet string will not support network addresses as channel bindings, and cautions that endpoint channel bindings should not be modeled as network addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo points to RFC 5056 for general security guidance. It warns that representing endpoint bindings as network addresses can make them unusable across language bindings.

references.text: Linn, J., "Generic Security Service Application Program Interface Version 2, Update 1", RFC 2743, January 2000.
Wray, J., "Generic Security Service API Version 2: C-bindings", RFC 2744, January 2000.
Williams, N., "On the Use of Channel Bindings to Secure Channels", RFC 5056, November 2007.
